q.m: Submission to Allah: outwardly the five pillars, inwardly the handing over of the whole self.
q.p: The word comes from a root carrying both surrender and peace, and the Qur'an calls it the religion with Allah (Qur'an 3:19). In the hadith of Jibril, islam is answered with the five pillars, iman with the six articles of belief, and ihsan with the quality of worship. So islam is the outward frame, iman the inner conviction, and ihsan the finish on both.

q.m: The belief that Allah is one, without partner, without equal, and alone deserving of worship.
q.p: The word means to make one, or to declare one. Surah al-Ikhlas states it in four short lines: He is One, the Eternal Refuge, He does not beget and was not begotten, and there is nothing comparable to Him (Qur'an 112). Tawhid is not only the claim that one God exists. It is that only He is worshipped.
q.q: Is Allah the same as God?

q.p: The Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe his Lord. The answer that came down is four short verses, and it is mostly a list of what He is not. He is not begotten. He does not beget. Nothing is comparable to Him. The shortest complete theology in the Book spends three quarters of itself clearing the ground.
q.q: What is Allah like? Does He have a form?

q.m: The set of things a Muslim holds to be true, as opposed to the things a Muslim does.
q.p: The root means to tie a knot, so aqidah is what the heart is tied to and does not untie. It covers Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree. Fiqh answers what you do; aqidah answers what you hold true.

q.m: The testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger.
q.p: It is the first of the five pillars and the door into Islam: whoever says it, understanding and meaning it, is a Muslim. It has two halves, which is why it is often called the shahadatain, the two testimonies. The first half empties the heart of every other object of worship; the second names the one man whose example shows how that worship is done. It is not a formula that works by sound. The scholars set conditions for it, among them knowledge of what it means, certainty rather than doubt, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance and acting on it.
q.q: How do I become a Muslim?

q.p: You said two sentences, ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah, and according to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself, everything before them was wiped from your record. Not archived. Wiped. When Amr ibn al-As came to pledge allegiance and hesitated over his past, the Prophet ﷺ told him: "Do you not know that Islam demolishes what came before it?" (Muslim 121).
q.q: I just said the shahada. What now?

q.m: The speech of Allah revealed to Muhammad in Arabic over about twenty three years, preserved word for word.
q.p: The word means the recitation, from a root meaning to read aloud. It is one book of 114 surahs, revealed piece by piece between Makkah and Madinah, memorised by the Companions and written down in the Prophet's lifetime. Muslims hold that the Arabic wording is itself the revelation, which is why any rendering into another language is called a translation of the meaning and never the Qur'an.

q.m: The gathering of the Qur'an into one written volume, carried out under Abu Bakr and then Uthman.
q.p: It was already written in the Prophet's lifetime on parchment, palm stalks and bone, and memorised by many Companions. After heavy losses among the reciters at the battle of Yamamah, Abu Bakr had Zayd ibn Thabit gather it into one set of sheets, which were later kept by Hafsah. Uthman then had standard copies made from those sheets and sent to the main cities, so that the whole community read from one text.

q.m: The scriptures Allah revealed, belief in them being one of the six articles of faith.
q.p: A Muslim believes that Allah spoke to earlier communities and that those revelations were true when they were given (Qur'an 2:285). The Qur'an names the Tawrat given to Musa, the Zabur to Dawud, the Injil to Isa, and pages given to Ibrahim and Musa. The mainstream position is that earlier scriptures were altered in wording or in handling over time, so present copies are not taken as authority, while the Qur'an is held to be the final one and preserved.
q.q: Do Muslims believe in the Bible and the Torah?

q.m: A report of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did, or quietly approved, passed down through named narrators.
q.p: The word means speech, or something newly told. A hadith has two parts: the chain of people who carried it, and the text they carried. A hadith is a report about the Sunnah, so a weak hadith does not become Sunnah by being printed in a book.

q.m: The Prophet's way in belief, worship and conduct, and the measure against which innovation is judged.
q.p: The word means a trodden path. In hadith study it covers what the Prophet peace be upon him said, did, and quietly approved; in fiqh it also names a recommended act; in creed it means the received way of the first generations, which is why the phrase Ahl al-Sunnah exists. Set against bid'ah, sunnah means the shape of the religion as it was handed over, rather than anyone's personal preference.

q.m: The formal Muslim prayer, performed five times a day at set times, facing Makkah.
q.p: The word means connection and supplication. Salah is a fixed sequence of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, with recitation from the Qur'an, done at five appointed times between dawn and night. It is the second pillar of Islam and the first act a person is asked about on the Day of Judgement. Persian and Urdu speakers usually call it namaz, which is the same thing.

q.m: The washing done before prayer: face, arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and feet to the ankles.
q.p: The four acts are named directly in the Qur'an, and the Prophet added rinsing the mouth and nose, washing the hands first, and doing each part three times. Wudu is broken by using the toilet, by passing wind, and by deep sleep; it is not broken by touching an animal or by ordinary dirt. One wudu lasts for as many prayers as you like until something breaks it.
q.q: Why do Muslims wash before praying?

q.m: The call announcing that a prayer time has entered, given aloud before each obligatory prayer.
q.p: It was taught to the companions in Madinah after they discussed how to gather people, and Bilal was its first caller. Its lines declare Allah's greatness, the testimony of faith, and the summons to prayer and to success. The Fajr adhan adds the line that prayer is better than sleep. The one who calls it is the muezzin.
q.q: What is that call you hear from mosques?

q.m: The direction of the Kaaba in Makkah, which Muslims face when they pray.
q.p: For sixteen or seventeen months in Madinah the Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem, and in the second year after the hijrah the Qur'an turned them to the Sacred Mosque. Those far from Makkah are asked for the direction rather than a perfect line, and someone with no way of knowing prays towards their best judgement and the prayer counts. Mosques mark it with a niche called the mihrab.
q.q: Which way do Muslims face, and why?

q.m: The stone cube at the centre of Makkah that Muslims face in every prayer.
q.p: The name comes from a word for a cube. The Qur'an describes Ibrahim and Isma'il raising its foundations, and calls it the first house appointed for mankind. Quraysh rebuilt it during the Prophet's youth and he settled their quarrel over who would set the Black Stone by carrying it on a cloak they all lifted together. Muslims face it, they do not worship it; it is a direction, and Umar said plainly of the Black Stone that it is a stone which neither harms nor benefits.

q.m: The Friday congregational prayer: a sermon followed by two rak'ahs, replacing Dhuhr.
q.p: The Qur'an commands believers to leave off trade and hurry to the remembrance of Allah when the Friday call is made. It is obligatory on adult resident men who are able to attend, and not obligatory on women, travellers or the sick, though all may attend. Whoever misses it prays Dhuhr as normal.

q.m: The yearly obligatory share of qualifying wealth, normally 2.5 percent, given to those entitled to it.
q.p: The word carries both purification and growth. Zakat is the third pillar, and the Qur'an names it beside the prayer again and again. It is due on savings, gold, silver and trade goods held for a lunar year above the nisab, at one fortieth of their value, while crops, livestock and mined wealth have their own rates. It is a debt owed to specific people, not a donation the giver may direct wherever they wish.

q.m: Fasting: abstaining from food, drink and intimacy from true dawn until sunset, with intention.
q.p: The word means to hold back. Fasting the month of Ramadan is the fourth pillar, and voluntary fasts are kept on other days through the year. The Qur'an sets its purpose as taqwa, God consciousness, and the Prophet warned that a fast without leaving off false speech is only hunger and thirst. Illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing, menstruation and old age all carry recognised concessions.

Ramadan is the ninth month, the one in which the Qur’an was sent down, and the only month named in the Book. This room is built to be worth opening on the third day and on the twenty seventh: what today asks of you, where you are in the reading, what the last ten nights are for, and the plain mechanics nobody quite explains. Every date here is calculated and your masjid’s announcement is the one that counts.

q.m: The night in Ramadan that the Qur'an calls better than a thousand months.
q.p: A whole surah is named for it, and it says worship in that one night is better than a thousand months, which is more than eighty years. It is sought in the last ten nights of Ramadan, and most strongly in the odd ones, with the twenty seventh most commonly named; the Prophet peace be upon him said to seek it rather than announced it, and the scholars read that hiding as mercy, so that the whole ten are revived. The du'a taught for it asks Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon.
q.q: What is the Night of Power?

q.p: There are two Eids and only two. Everything else a Muslim community celebrates is a custom, which is not a criticism, only an accurate description. This one room holds both of them, because most of what they ask of you is identical: the same takbir, the same washing and the same best clothes, the same two rak’ahs with no call to prayer, the same sermon afterwards, the same instruction to take a different road home, the same absolute prohibition on fasting the day itself.

Al-Hajj, the pilgrimage, is the fifth pillar of Islam and the one journey a Muslim makes once in a life if he is able. This room is written for someone who has never gone: what you do, on which day, in what order, what is a pillar and what is only better, where the schools of law differ, and what to do when something goes wrong.

q.m: Forbidden. Leaving it is rewarded, and doing it deliberately is a sin.
q.p: The list is far shorter than people assume: shirk, killing, theft, interest, intoxicants, pork, gambling, zina, and injustice to others. Something is haram only on clear evidence, and calling a disputed matter haram is itself a serious step, since the Qur'an warns against declaring things lawful and unlawful without knowledge. The same root also means sacred and inviolable, which is why the mosque in Makkah is al-Masjid al-Haram.
q.q: What is actually forbidden in Islam?

q.m: Permitted. Anything revelation has not forbidden, which is the great majority of things.
q.p: The word means loosed or untied. In ordinary worldly matters the default is permission, so the burden of proof lies on whoever claims a thing is forbidden, not on the person doing it. In food it usually means meat slaughtered properly and free of pork, blood and intoxicants. But halal covers earnings, speech and work at least as much as it covers dinner.

q.m: Intoxicants. Wine and anything else that clouds the mind, forbidden in the Qur'an.
q.p: The prohibition arrived in stages, ending with the command to shun it as a defilement from the work of Satan. The Prophet's rule that whatever intoxicates in large amounts is forbidden in small amounts extends the ban to every intoxicant, and it is the textbook example of qiyas at work. Hanafis kept the word khamr technically for grape wine while forbidding other intoxicants under a separate heading, arriving at the same practical result. Scholars differ over intoxicating substances used as medicine where no alternative exists.

q.m: Interest or unjust increase on a loan or exchange, forbidden in the Qur'an in severe terms.
q.p: Two forms are named: riba al-fadl, an unequal swap of the same commodity hand to hand, and riba al-nasi'ah, the increase charged for time, which is what an interest bearing loan involves. The Qur'an permits trade and forbids riba in the same breath, and the objection is to money multiplying from money with no shared risk and no real goods. Scholars differ sharply over how far the ruling extends into modern banking, and Islamic finance is the attempt to answer that.

q.m: The covering a Muslim woman wears in public, most often a headscarf with modest clothing.
q.p: The command to draw the khimar over the neckline stands in Surah al-Nur, directly after the command to believing men to lower their gaze; the outer garment, the jilbab, is in Surah al-Ahzab. The word itself means a screen or curtain, and in the Qur'an it usually means a barrier rather than a garment; the everyday sense of headscarf is later usage. The schools agree on covering the hair and body and differ over the face and hands.
q.q: Why do Muslim women wear hijab?

q.p: Spiritually, the Qur'an flattens every hierarchy: it lists believing men and believing women side by side ten times in a single verse and promises both "forgiveness and an immense reward" (Al-Ahzab 33:35). The most knowledgeable transmitter of the Prophet's ﷺ private sunnah was a woman, Aisha, whom senior companions consulted. The world's oldest continuously operating university, al-Qarawiyyin in Fes, was founded by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, in 859.
q.q: What does Islam say about women?

q.m: The whole of what God revealed as guidance: belief, worship, character and law together.
q.p: The word literally means the path to water, and the Qur'an uses it for the way God set out for the Prophet to follow. It is far wider than law in the modern sense; most of it concerns prayer, fasting, honesty and family, and only a small portion concerns courts and punishment. Shari'ah is the revelation itself, while fiqh is the scholarly understanding of it, and collapsing the two makes human opinion sound divine.

The Qur'an calls marriage a mithaq ghaliz, a heavy covenant (4:21). The same weight of phrase is used for the pact Allah took from the prophets. That is the register: not a party, not a transaction between families, but a solemn undertaking witnessed before Allah.

q.m: Turning back to Allah from a sin: stopping it, regretting it, and resolving not to return.
q.p: The Qur'an calls for a sincere turning, tawbatan nasuha (Qur'an 66:8). Scholars list the conditions as leaving the sin, regretting it, resolving not to repeat it, and, where a person's right was taken, returning it or seeking their pardon. The Prophet peace be upon him said every child of Adam errs, and the best of those who err are those who repent, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Falling again does not cancel the earlier repentance; it calls for another one.
q.q: What if I have done something terrible?

q.m: Giving to something other than Allah what belongs to Allah alone, above all worship.
q.p: The word means to make a partner or to share. The Qur'an says Allah does not forgive that a partner be set up with Him, and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills (Qur'an 4:48). Commentators read that of the one who dies without repenting, since the Qur'an elsewhere promises forgiveness to whoever turns back. Scholars distinguish major shirk, which takes a person outside Islam, from minor shirk, which is a grave sin but does not.
q.q: What is the one sin that isn't forgiven?

q.m: Allah's decree: that He knows, wrote, willed and created all that happens, without forcing anyone to sin.
q.p: Scholars describe four levels to it: Allah's knowledge of everything, its writing in the Preserved Tablet, His will, and His creating it. The Qur'an says He created every thing in due measure (Qur'an 54:49), and the word itself carries measure rather than blind fate. Belief in qadr is the sixth article of faith in the hadith of Jibril. It does not remove your choice and it is not a reason to stop trying, which is why the Prophet peace be upon him answered a question about it by telling the man to act.
q.q: Is everything already decided? Do I have a choice?

q.m: Asking Allah directly, in any language, at any time, for anything permitted.
q.p: The Qur'an says call on Me and I will answer you (Qur'an 40:60), and the Prophet peace be upon him said du'a is worship itself, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Scholars describe three possible answers: the thing asked for, something equal or better kept back for later, or a harm turned away. He also warned against impatience, saying a servant is answered as long as he does not say I asked and was not answered, in Bukhari and Muslim.

q.m: Angels: beings created from light who never disobey Allah and carry out exactly what they are commanded.
q.p: Belief in them is one of the six articles of faith. Their creation from light is reported in Sahih Muslim rather than in the Qur'an. They are not male or female in the human sense, they do not eat or tire, and the Qur'an says they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are told (Qur'an 66:6). A few are named in the texts, most are not, and their number is known to Allah alone.

q.m: A created race made from fire, unseen to us, who like people believe or disbelieve and are accountable.
q.p: The Qur'an gives them a surah of their own (Qur'an 72), reports a group of them listening to the recitation and accepting it, and says they were created from a smokeless flame of fire (Qur'an 55:15). They eat, they marry, they die, and they will be judged. They are not the spirits of dead humans, and they are not behind most of what gets blamed on them.

q.m: A devil: any rebellious jinn, and with the definite article, Iblis himself.
q.p: The Qur'an says he is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy (Qur'an 35:6), and gives him only two tools, whispering and inviting. He cannot compel anyone; on the Day of Judgement he tells his own followers that he had no authority over them except that he called and they answered (Qur'an 14:22). The Qur'an also calls some human beings shayatin, so the word is not limited to jinn.
q.q: How much power does the devil have?

q.p: Sihr is real, and it is smaller than you have been told. This room holds what the Qur’an actually says, the free protection the Prophet ﷺ taught to everyone, ruqya you can do yourself tonight, the myths that cost people their money and their marriages, and the part nobody says out loud: a trained body carries a steadier heart.
q.q: Is magic real? Is the evil eye real?

q.p: The Qur’an and the Sunnah map this road in detail: the last breath, the leaving of the soul, the washing and the prayer of the living, the grave and its questioning, the long barzakh, the Trumpet, the gathering, the scales, the bridge and the two homes. None of it was revealed to frighten you, but so that a believer travels a road already drawn, toward a Lord already known, and so that grief, when it comes, has somewhere true to stand.

q.m: Paradise: the garden of lasting delight prepared for the believers, where nothing is lost or spoiled.
q.p: The word means a garden covered over by its own foliage, and the Qur'an describes rivers, shade and gardens, then says the pleasure of Allah is greater than all of it (Qur'an 9:72). A sacred hadith describes what is in it as what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined. Firdaws is named as its highest part, beneath the Throne. In Sunni belief its greatest gift is the sight of Allah Himself.

q.m: The Fire: the punishment prepared for those who refused, described in the Qur'an in plain and heavy terms.
q.p: The Qur'an gives it names and levels and says the Fire was prepared for those who reject faith (Qur'an 2:24). Sunni belief holds that believers who enter it for their sins do not remain in it, and are brought out by mercy and intercession, while disbelief carried to the grave meets a lasting punishment. The verses are not decoration, and they are also not an invitation to guess who is going there.

q.m: The Day of Resurrection, when this creation ends, the dead are raised, and everyone is judged.
q.p: The word means the standing, because people stand before their Lord. Its timing is known to Allah alone, though the Prophet peace be upon him described signs that come before it. The Qur'an returns to this Day constantly, not to frighten, but because a life that ends in an account is lived differently from one that does not.
q.q: What is the Day of Judgement?

q.m: The signs that come before the Day of Judgement, sorted by scholars into minor and major.
q.p: The Qur'an says its signs have already come (Qur'an 47:18), which commentators read as the sending of the final Prophet. The minor signs are gradual changes in society described across the hadith literature; the major ones are the ten listed in a report in Sahih Muslim, among them the Dajjal, the descent of Isa, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the beast, the smoke, the sun rising from the west, and a fire that drives people to their final gathering. Reading current events as the fulfilment of signs is an old habit, and every attempt to put a date on it has been wrong so far.
q.q: What are the signs before the end?

q.p: Twenty-five are named in the Qur'an. But the chain of light is vastly longer: "We sent messengers before you: of some We have told you their story, and of some We have not told you." A well-known narration of Abu Dharr counts one hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets across humanity. Every people, every valley, every forgotten age: someone stood up among them and said the same words: worship Allah alone.
q.q: How many prophets are there in Islam?

q.m: The descent of Isa near the end of time, to break the cross, kill the Dajjal, and rule with justice.
q.p: The Qur'an says he was not killed and not crucified, but that Allah raised him (Qur'an 4:157-158), and calls him a sign of the Hour (Qur'an 43:61). The hadiths describe his descent, his prayer behind the leader of the Muslims, and his death and burial afterwards like any other human being. He returns as a follower of the final Prophet, not with a new religion.
q.q: Do Muslims believe in Jesus? Was he crucified?

q.p: On the ninth of Dhul Hijjah in the year 10 AH the Prophet ﷺ rode into the valley at Arafah and spoke to the largest gathering of his life, about a hundred thousand pilgrims who had come to learn their Hajj from him. It was his last public address, given roughly three months before his death, and he delivered it like a man setting his house in order while there was still time.
q.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ say at the end of his life?

q.p: Every conversation about Islam's divisions should begin with an embarrassing fact for the dividers: the overwhelming mass of the religion is held in common by everyone who prays toward Makkah. Before a single difference is named, a Muslim of any school believes in Allah alone, His angels, His Books, His messengers, the Last Day and the decree; prays five times toward one House; fasts one month; gives one alms; recites one Qur'an, letter for letter, from Jakarta to Casablanca.
q.q: What is the difference between Sunni and Shia?

q.m: A school of law: a settled method of deriving rulings, carried by generations of scholars.
q.p: The plural is madhahib, and the word means a way gone along. Four Sunni schools survive with a living scholarly tradition: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. They agree on the pillars and on the great majority of rulings, and differ mostly in method and in detail. A madhhab is not a sect, and a Hanafi and a Shafi'i pray behind one another without difficulty.
q.q: What are the four schools of law?

q.m: The Islamic tradition of inner purification, called Sufism in English, and read very differently by different scholars.
q.p: At its origin the word names the science of the heart: sincerity, remembrance, character and struggle against the self, as taught by early figures such as al-Junayd and later organised by al-Ghazali. Over the centuries it also grew orders, practices and claims that other scholars judged to be innovations, and opinion today runs from full acceptance to full rejection, with many holding the content sound wherever it stays inside the Book and the Sunnah. When you meet the word it helps to ask which is meant: the subject matter, or a particular order and what it does.

q.m: People who lived without a prophet's message reaching them, and the question of how they are judged.
q.p: The Qur'an says We do not punish until We have sent a messenger (Qur'an 17:15), which every school takes as the starting point. The Ash'ari position is that such a person is not punished, because obligation begins when the message arrives, while Maturidis hold that reason alone still obliges a person to recognise the Creator. A well known group of hadiths describes them being tested on the Day of Judgement itself, and many scholars, including within the Hanbali tradition, hold that view. What all sides agree on is that these are cases for Allah to judge, and not a category for living people to sort each other into.
q.q: What happens to people who never heard of Islam?
